card.hook: Most people dive straight into the fish aisles and never find out the market has a calm, breezy back porch. Walk through to the water side and you get the whole building with ships behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the seaside area behind the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road. Face the building's seaward side and keep a strip of harbour in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the building with the water behind it. Try 0.5x to fit the whole length of the building and a big sweep of harbour. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one ship or a detail on the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the building on one third of the frame with water and ships filling the rest, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the harbour is easy to see. Wait for a gap in the passers-by before you shoot, and if you're here in autumn, the Busan Jagalchi Festival may add some extra colour.
card.selfie_here: Pose in front of the Jagalchi Market sign at the building's street-side entrance (52 Jagalchihaean-ro, Jung-gu). Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the sign over your shoulder so the name is in the shot. This spot comes from one photo caption, so have a look around when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the market are generally fine, but ask permission before taking close-ups of people. Don't block the narrow walkways between stalls to line up a shot in busy hours. The seaside area behind the market is a free public space, but the market's own opening days vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the market building, a strip of water and one ship all in the same frame, with nobody's elbow in it.
card.good_to_know: Jagalchi is generally considered the largest fish market in South Korea, and it sits on the edge of Nampo Port. The name is said to come from jagal, the Korean word for gravel, because gravel once surrounded the market. It's also known for the "Jagalchi Ajumma", the female vendors, a name that goes back to the years after the Korean War, when women sold goods on the streets here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: the seaside area behind the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road. Face the building's seaward side and keep a strip of harbour in the frame.

card.hook: Picture a long, wide sweep of sand with a wall of high-rise towers standing right behind it. That's Haeundae, and your phone will love it. There's plenty of room to step back and fit the lot in.
card.stand_here: Head for the seafront near 해운대해변로 and stand about 170 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of sand, sea and towers. Switch to 1x for people and umbrellas, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the high-rises or a detail on the sand.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line so it stays level, and add footprints or the edge of a wave in the foreground.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. After dark, try night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
card.selfie_here: Find the Haeundae Beach sign on the sand and stand beside it with the sea and skyline behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more of the backdrop in, and hold the phone a little low.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at a coastal lookout on Dongbaek Island to frame you with the whole beach curving behind; no exact spot is known, so pick a place where the full beach is in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Events can change what's on the sand, so check the official site before you go if you're visiting during a festival.
card.challenge: Take a shot where your footprints lead toward the sea, with one tall tower tucked to the side of the frame, not in the middle.
card.good_to_know: Haeundae opened as a beach in 1965 and was the largest in the country at the time. It was a fishing area before that, and has been a leisure space since the late 19th century. In 2008 it set a Guinness World Record for the most beach umbrellas, 7,937.

card.hook: A small Little Prince and his fox sit on a terrace while a whole hillside of pastel houses tumbles away behind them, and yes, half the village is queuing to photograph them. It's worth joining the queue.
card.stand_here: Head for the Little Prince viewpoint, the terrace with the Little Prince and Fox statue, roughly midway along the main walking route. The heart of the village is to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. Face out over the rooftops toward the sea, with the statue close to you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the statue, or for a friend sitting beside it. Tap 0.5x to fit more of the layered rooftops in. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it to pick out one group of colourful houses.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on one side, and leave the rooftops and sea to fill the rest of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset means a shorter queue at the statue. Shops and cafes reportedly close around six and some inner lanes are partly unlit after dark, so check current opening times before planning a late visit.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the ledge beside the Little Prince and Fox statue with the hillside rooftops behind you. Use the front camera and keep your arm out so the view fits over your shoulder. For a second go, stand by the red I ♥ Gamcheon sign on the walking route, with the colourful houses behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the road on the south side of the village, by the Avant Garde Cafe, facing north so the whole hillside of houses is in the frame (you don't need to go into the cafés), and check the framing when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The alleys have many narrow, steep stairs, so take care as you move around. It's an open neighbourhood where people live, and you should check the official site before you go for current access details.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the Little Prince looks like he's quietly judging the queue behind you.
card.good_to_know: The village was built in the 1920s and 1930s. A public art project that began in 2009 turned it into the colourful place you see today, with sculptures, murals and small installations added by art students, artists and residents. It's sometimes nicknamed "Korea's Santorini".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Little Prince viewpoint, the terrace with the Little Prince and Fox statue, roughly midway along the main walking route. card.hook: Most temples hide away in the mountains, but this one has its toes in the sea. Golden roofs, stone steps and open water all squeeze into one picture, so your phone is going to have a very good day.
card.stand_here: Stand on Yongmun-gyo, the bridge leading to the main hall, and turn around to shoot back toward the halls. You'll see the golden-roofed halls stacked on the rocks with the sea behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the temple and the sea into one frame, then try 1x for a more natural view. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out lanterns, roof details and carvings without leaving your spot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, because the sea makes any tilt obvious.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and less crowded. Around Buddha's Birthday the paper lanterns make everything more colourful, but expect a lot more people.
card.selfie_here: Head to the viewpoint beside the Haesu Gwaneum Daebul statue, on the cliff terrace around the big golden Buddha, facing the East Sea. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the temple buildings and sea come over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Go down to the lower rocks at the water's edge below the main hall (Daeungjeon), stand on the rocks in front, and ask a passer-by to shoot back up so the wooden hall and cliff fill the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your voice low and leave space for worshippers. Photos are fine from the doorway of the main hall, but don't disrupt any ceremony. This is a working temple, so dress modestly. The stairs are steep in places, so wear comfy shoes.
card.challenge: Find a paper lantern and line it up so the sea sits right behind it, then take three shots and keep your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Haedong Yonggungsa is a Buddhist temple on the coast of Gijang-gun, in the east of Busan. It's one of few temples in Korea set right beside the sea. The temple says it was first built in 1376, though that date is disputed, and it honours Haesu Gwaneum Daebul, the Sea Goddess Buddha of Mercy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Yongmun-gyo, the bridge leading to the main hall, and turn around to shoot back toward the halls. You'll see the golden-roofed halls stacked on the rocks with the sea behind them.

card.hook: Here's a nice surprise: the bridge does all the hard work for you. Walk onto the sand at Gwangalli Beach and the whole Gwangan Bridge stretches across the bay, ready for its close-up.
card.stand_here: Stand about 290 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be on Gwangalli Beach, in the central section on the sand just above the waterline.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the bridge across the bay with the beach below it. Go 0.5x for more sand and promenade in front, but the bridge will look smaller. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the bridge and its lights closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line so the bridge sits across the middle, and keep your phone level so the bridge doesn't slope.
card.best_time: Aim for blue hour, about 20 to 30 minutes after sunset, when the bridge lights are on and the colours are richest. At dusk, use night mode, tuck your elbows in to stay steady, tap the bridge, then slide the picture a little darker so the lights don't wash out.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Ryan and Chunshik photo zone, the big figure sculptures on the sand, and pose with the bridge behind them. People line up for this one, so be patient. Use the front camera (or 0.5x) and keep the bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand in the middle of the beach with you in front of them and the sea and bridge behind you, so the full bridge span fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Shoot only from pedestrian areas open to visitors. Stay off the bridge access roads and don't stop on a shoulder for photos.
card.challenge: Take one photo with the bridge perfectly level, then one where you sneak the waterline along the bottom. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Gwangalli Beach is a curved, half-moon stretch of fine sand about 1.4 km long, tucked inside a cove that the Gwangan Bridge spans. It's remembered as a location for the car chase in the 2018 film Black Panther. On Saturdays a free drone show is held over the bay and draws large crowds, so arrive well before it starts.

card.hook: Picture a mermaid sitting on the rocks, gazing out at the sea, and you're about to take her portrait. That's Princess Hwangok, and she's the best place to start on Dongbaek Island.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the rocks by the shoreline, below the coastal path. Face the statue so the open sea is behind her.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the statue and plenty of sea both fit. If you can't get close enough, try zoom 2x to fill the frame with her. Use zoom 0.5x only when you want loads of sky and sea.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on one line, then tap the bright sea and slide it darker until she turns into a dark shape against glowing water.
card.best_time: Early morning is when one guide recommends this statue, because the light is soft. Save the lighthouse view for golden hour.
card.selfie_here: Head to the coastal boardwalk next to the Mermaid Statue, which one guide recommends for soft morning photos. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and turn so the statue is over your shoulder. For a sunset selfie, go to the white lighthouse at the island's tip and face the open sea.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the beach at the western end of Haeundae Beach, near the Westin Josun, and shoot east so the headland fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a military-protected area, so some coastal views are restricted. Follow the signs and stay on the path. Check opening hours at the lighthouse and APEC House before you go. Motorbikes and bicycles can't go onto the island, and watch your head on low branches on the forest trail.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the statue with her on the left, in the middle and on the right, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Dongbaekseom used to be a true island, but soil built up between it and the shore, so it's now part of the mainland. The name comes from camellia flowers, which are said to bloom here in large numbers. Busan made it a designated monument in 1999, and the poet Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn is recorded as having visited.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the rocks by the shoreline, below the coastal path. Face the statue so the open sea is behind her.

card.hook: Huinnyeoul is the kind of village where the sea keeps popping up between the houses, like it's playing peekaboo. Keep your phone out, because you'll want it every few steps.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Isongdo Observatory terrace (이송도전망대), next to the piano stairs on the village path, and face the open sea. To find it, take the alley just before the piano stairs.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the sea, the greenery and the stairway together. Tap 0.5x if the terrace is busy or you want more of the stairs, or try 2x (higher depends on your phone) for a tighter view of the sea and the steps below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, and tap the sea so the bright water keeps its colour (drag the slider to make it a little darker if it looks washed out).
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light than midday. The tunnel and rainbow stairs also tend to be quieter at less busy times of day.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the entrance of the Huinnyeoul Coastal Tunnel, on the coastal promenade, with the ocean and city skyline behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the landmark over your shoulder. Some guides also like the tunnel exit, where the bright sea is framed by the dark tunnel.
card.rules_and_safety: On the coastal trail, watch out for waves, wind and wet surfaces. The lower coastal route involves climbing stairs, so wear comfortable shoes, and check conditions on the day.
card.challenge: Count how many different 'sea peeking between the buildings' shots you can find on the way down, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Guides treat the Isongdo Observatory (also called the Huinnyeoul Observatory) as the village's main photo spot. Inside the coastal tunnel you can shoot a silhouette or portrait against the bright sea, and Namhang Bridge is sometimes visible in the opening. The village and its viewpoints are open public space and free to enter.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Isongdo Observatory terrace (이송도전망대), next to the piano stairs on the village path, and face the open sea. To find it, take the alley just before the piano stairs.

selfie_spots.why: Guides call the tunnel entrance the most popular pose spot, and it gives a sea-and-skyline backdrop that many visitors queue to use.

Some sources are older blogs (one dated about 1,900 days ago), and the Piano Stairs and tunnel names come from different sites. Source-based page on the tunnel exit describes the best-known lower-route shot but does not give a precise spot. The sea-facing and tunnel photos depend on daylight and weather.

card.hook: Ask ten people how many islands Oryukdo has and the tide gets a vote. The name means 'Five-Six Islands' because the count changes depending on how the rocks look from shore.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the U-shaped glass walkway at the Oryukdo Skywalk and face south, straight out to sea. Guides name the centre of the U as the best single photo position.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the walkway and the sea on both sides, then go to 1x for the islets straight ahead. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull in the lighthouse island.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, and leave the islets just off-centre.
card.best_time: One guide suggests weekday mornings around 10-11am, when the light is less backlit. The glass floor closes in rain or strong wind, so check the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the outer curve of the horseshoe-shaped glass walkway so the islets are right behind you, then use the front camera and hold your phone firmly. A reviewer says the best sea views are from the stairs on the left just before the walkway, so try a selfie there too (check which stairs when you arrive).
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand on the hill in the park next to the skywalk, where they can frame the skywalk and the islands together, while you wave from the walkway.
card.rules_and_safety: Shoe covers are required on the glass floor and are provided at the entrance. Visitors report that selfie sticks aren't allowed on the glass walkway, so keep it to your phone. The skywalk can close in strong wind or rain, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the islets, then check again after a few minutes and see if you get a different number.
card.good_to_know: Only the outermost island, Deungdaeseom, is built on, and it carries a lighthouse. The rocks come from volcanic activity about 80 million years ago. The islets are protected and nobody can visit them, which is why you photograph them from the shore. The Skywalk opened in 2013.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the U-shaped glass walkway at the Oryukdo Skywalk and face south, straight out to sea. Guides name the centre of the U as the best single photo position.

selfie_spots.why: Standing on the outer curve puts the islets directly behind you, which frames a selfie with the landmark.

card.hook: Gukje Market doesn't give you one big view, and that's the fun of it. It's about 400 m across, so you get hanging signs, stacked goods and narrow lanes, and you go hunting for the good bits.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon near 자갈치해안로, about 340 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. Once you're inside, stand at a lane junction where you can see two or three directions at once.
card.zoom: Use 0.5x for narrow lanes and long views between stalls, and 1x for most stall and street scenes. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for signs and goods from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a lane up so it runs toward the centre of the frame, with a stall on each side and a walking person or bright sign for scale.
card.best_time: A weekday morning is usually calmer, so you get more open lanes. Late afternoon into evening brings lit signs, so switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Look for the replica of the Kkotbunine shop from the film, inside Building B between Zone 3 and Zone 4. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and pose with the signboard over your shoulder. Busanpedia says the shop has recently changed to a cafe, so the signboard may be different or gone. Check before you go.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before taking close-up photos of stallholders or customers, and step aside from busy walkways when you stop to frame a shot.
card.challenge: Find a lane where the stalls repeat on both sides, then catch one person walking through the middle of your frame.
card.good_to_know: Gukje Market started in 1945 as Dottaegi Market, a name that roughly means 'bustling market', and took its present name in 1950. Refugees arriving in Busan during the Korean War set up stalls here, and a fire in 1953 badly damaged it. Many visitors know the name from the 2014 film Ode to My Father, which takes its Korean title from the market.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon near 자갈치해안로, about 340 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. Once you're inside, stand at a lane junction where you can see two or three directions at once.

selfie_spots.why: The replica of the film's shop is a well-known photo stop, and visitors pose in front of its signboard.

card.hook: Busan Tower is so tall and skinny that your first photo will probably be of its feet and a lot of sky. Don't worry, everyone does it, and the fix is easy.
card.stand_here: Head into Yongdusan Park in Jung District. The phone icon sits right at the foot of the tower, so you'll need to walk a little way back along the park paths until the whole tower fits. Look for a gap in the trees and people, then face the tower.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x if you're close to the base and want to look up at the whole thing. Zoom 1x from a few steps back gives a more natural shape. Save zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower and the deck.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's sides up with a vertical line so it stands tall and straight.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime for a clear view of the tower, and of the port from the deck. Around dusk, switch on night mode if the tower is lit, and rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady. The deck and cafe only open during working hours, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the outdoor plaza below the tower in Yongdusan Park, with the tower rising directly behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and step back slightly so the full height fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand near the octagonal pavilion next to the tower and face the tower, then pose so the pavilion's traditional roofline and the tower both fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Yongdusan Park is slightly elevated, so older visitors and children should travel light and watch their footing.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three different distances, then pick the one where the tower looks like it's trying to poke a cloud.
card.good_to_know: The tower is 120 metres tall and was built in 1973. It's purely for sightseeing and has no transmitting equipment. Two high-speed elevators take you up to the deck, and the base is linked to a few galleries and souvenir shops.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Yongdusan Park in Jung District. The phone icon sits right at the foot of the tower, so you'll need to walk a little way back along the park paths until the whole tower fits. Look for a gap in the trees and people, then face the tower.

selfie_spots.why: The open plaza gives a clear, centred backdrop of the tower for a portrait, and a little distance keeps the whole structure in the frame.

card.hook: You can't stroll across the Diamond Bridge, because it's cars only, so the trick is to find a good spot on the shore. The coastal path at Dongbaekseom is a quieter choice than the beach, and it puts a headland, a building and an island in your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at 누리마루 APEC하우스, on the coastal path observation deck around Dongbaekseom on the Haeundae side. Face the bridge so Nurimaru APEC House sits beside it and Oryukdo island is further to the left. From Dongbaek Station Exit 1 it's about a 20-minute walk to the deck by the APEC House.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the bridge and the coast fit in one frame. Switch to 0.5x if you want the APEC House and Oryukdo in too. For a tighter shot of the bridge, which is a long way off, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge on the lower line, leaving sky and sea above it.
card.best_time: Go around dusk, when the bridge lights come on and the sky still has some colour. The lighting schedule changes with the season and the day, so check it before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the Gwangalli Beach promenade, in a stretch with fewer people. Use the front camera (0.5x gets more in) and keep the Gwangan Bridge behind you as your backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone who stands on the sand near the middle of Gwangalli Beach, facing the bridge, while you stand between them and the bridge so the whole span shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Walking or cycling across the bridge isn't allowed, so stay on the beach and promenade for your photos. Check the official site for any visiting rules at Nurimaru APEC House itself.
card.challenge: Can you get the bridge, the APEC House and Oryukdo island all in one shot, with the bridge sitting neatly on a gridline?
card.good_to_know: Gwangan Bridge, also called the Diamond Bridge, is a double-decked suspension bridge linking Haeundae and Suyeong across the bay. It's 7,420 metres long, which makes it the second longest bridge in South Korea. Building started in 1994 and finished in December 2002. It opened briefly for the 2002 Asian Games, then officially in January 2003.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at 누리마루 APEC하우스, on the coastal path observation deck around Dongbaekseom on the Haeundae side. Face the bridge so Nurimaru APEC House sits beside it and Oryukdo island is further to the left. From Dongbaek Station Exit 1 it's about a 20-minute walk to the deck by the APEC House.

The passer-by spot is inferred from a page describing the straight-on view from the sand; no page names a specific photographer position for a visitor with the whole bridge in frame. The Hello Gwangalli red sign on the sand is described with the bridge in front, so it was not used as a selfie spot.

card.hook: Most spots have one big star. Taejongdae has a whole forest of evergreens, then a lighthouse, then the sea, so your photo is really about layers of green and open sky.
card.stand_here: Stand about 560 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then take a few steps either side and compare the views before you pick your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the trees, paths and general scene. Go to 0.5x for big open outlooks, and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the lighthouse or ships far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third, with a railing, path or tree branch in the foreground to add depth.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the trees than midday. Check the weather first, because haze can flatten the distant views.
card.selfie_here: Try the Sinseon Rock cliff, below Yeongdo Lighthouse. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the lighthouse and cliffs in the frame behind your shoulder. If you'd rather stay inside, the first floor of the round observatory is quieter than the upper floors.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the bronze mother-and-child statue beside the observatory and ask a passer-by to frame you with the lighthouse and cliffs behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Sinseon Rock is reached by a short side path and can be closed, so check the official site for current access. Watch your footing on wet rocks, since the rocky shoreline is reached by short side trails.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: dark green trees at the front, a railing or path in the middle, and the sea or sky behind, with the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: Taejongdae is a big natural park at the southern tip of Yeongdo District, so allow time to walk because the best views are rarely beside the entrance. The name is linked to King Taejong Muyeol of Silla, who is said to have enjoyed practising archery here. The park is listed as Busan monument number 28, together with Oryukdo Island.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 560 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then take a few steps either side and compare the views before you pick your frame.

card.hook: Picture a cable car gliding over a sandy curve of beach while you stand on a glass floor above the waves. That's Songdo, and yes, your stomach may notice the glass.
card.stand_here: Stand on 송도 구름산책로 (the Songdo Cloud Walkway), at the beach end by the Songdo Bay cable car station. The beach is about 1 minute on foot to the east. From the glass-floored stretch, face the curved shoreline with the cable cars crossing overhead.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the curve of the shoreline. Go to 0.5x when you want the walkway, the sea and the cable cars all in one frame. Try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out a single cable car against the sky or the sand.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the curve of the beach along the lower third, then tap the sand or a cable car and drag the slider down a little to make it darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the walkway. At dusk, switch on night mode and steady your phone against the rail.
card.selfie_here: Head for the half turtle-egg-shell seat on the Songdo Cloud Trails skywalk, on the eastern side of the beach near Songdo Bay Station, where you look out over the ocean with the beach in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the sea and coast over your shoulder. The glass-floor sections also make a fun backdrop, though it's best to check which way the view faces on the day.
card.ask_someone: You could ask a passer-by on the Yongso islet causeway bridge, about halfway along the Songdo Coastal Road, to take your photo, but check the view first because we haven't confirmed it frames the whole beach.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep a firm grip on your phone when you lean over the rail or the glass floor. The walkway is free, but coastal boardwalks can close for repairs after storms, so check current access before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a cable car in the top of your frame with one tiny person on the sand below, then see if your friends can spot them.
card.good_to_know: Songdo Beach was created by people in 1913 and was the first public beach in Korea. Songdo means 'Island of Pines', after the thick pine forest that once covered the island. A cable car has crossed over the beach to Geobuk (Turtle) Island since 1964, and cable cars still cross the bay today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on 송도 구름산책로 (the Songdo Cloud Walkway), at the beach end by the Songdo Bay cable car station. The beach is about 1 minute on foot to the east. From the glass-floored stretch, face the curved shoreline with the cable cars crossing overhead.

card.hook: Down in the Nampo-dong streets, the signs are shouting at you from every side and your photo ends up looking like a neon fruit salad. The fix is simple: go up.
card.stand_here: Head up to the viewing platform on the upper floors of Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장) and face the harbour, with the port and bridge ahead and the Nampo-dong waterfront below you. It's described as facing the harbour, so check it's open when you arrive.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the port, the bridge and the waterfront in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the bridge or the boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the harbour and bridge fill most of the frame.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, and try late afternoon, when the light over the harbour turns softer. Check the platform is open before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the far end of the Nampo-dong alley that leads to Yeongdodaegyo Bridge, which is a popular photo stop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Over at the Busan Tower plaza in Yongdusan Park, ask a passer-by to stand a little back from the plaza below the tower and shoot upward, while you stand in the centre with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch out for crowds at Yeongdo Bridge when it lifts, and use the designated photo areas. Jagalchi Market is a working market, so check its official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the bridge, a boat and a slice of the Nampo-dong waterfront all in one shot, with the horizon on that upper third line.
card.good_to_know: Nampo-dong is Busan's busy central shopping district, in Jung District right beside the harbour. Heading south, the shopping streets turn into Kangtong Market, Gukje Market and then Jagalchi Market, where seafood is sold and served. Two bridges link the area to Yeongdo District across the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the viewing platform on the upper floors of Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장) and face the harbour, with the port and bridge ahead and the Nampo-dong waterfront below you. It's described as facing the harbour, so check it's open when you arrive.

Busan Tower stands in Yongdusan Park near Nampo-dong, not inside it, so the ask-someone spot is outside the district. The Gwangbok-ro entry is a photo caption, not written advice. card.hook: Picture a green hillside where every white marker lines up like it's been measured with a ruler. That's the pull here: calm, order, and flags standing tall above it all.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, along the central paths between the national plots, looking down the rows of graves. The subject lies a short way to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the rows and the flags in one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single flag above the markers, and use 0.5x only for the whole curved wall, keeping the horizon level.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put a path or row of markers on a line leading into the frame, then tap the brightest white marker and slide a little darker so the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits white markers and avoids glare. There's a daily flag ceremony, but sources disagree on the times, so check when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Head to the flag-lined symbolic area just inside the entrance and stand with the national flags behind you. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if you want more flags in), hold the phone a little low, and keep it quick and quiet.
card.rules_and_safety: Outdoor photos are generally fine, but not inside the memorial hall. Stay off the grass and grave boundaries, keep quiet, skip drones, and avoid photographing people or ceremonies. Check with the office before publishing or selling photos.
card.challenge: Find the path where the rows of markers lead your eye straight to a flag, and get that one clean, quiet shot.
card.good_to_know: This is the only United Nations cemetery in the world. About 2,300 Korean War servicemembers' graves sit on roughly 14 hectares, grouped into 22 plots by nationality. The curved Wall of Remembrance, finished in 2006, carries 40,896 names on 140 marble panels around a central fountain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, along the central paths between the national plots, looking down the rows of graves. The subject lies a short way to the north-east.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole cemetery in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. Neither selfie spot is described by any page as a photo spot; both are named areas that I matched to a selfie. No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods. No page gives a safety point. One Duffelbag review objects to guests taking selfies at the site, so keep selfies brief and quiet. Sources disagree on flag times (10am raising and 4pm lowering in reviews; 5pm lowering in one blog), so check on arrival.
